Figure 1. We introduce Capability-Conditioned Navigation (CapNav), a benchmark designed to evaluate how well VLMs can navigate
complex indoor spaces given an agent’s specific physical and operational capabilities. CapNav inputs (1) a tour video of an indoor space,
(2) nodes of its navigation graph, (3) an agent’s mobility profile, and (4) a navigation task, and evaluates VLM outputs in task feasibility,
path validity, route traversability, and reasoning validity.



                            Abstract                                                 based on agent capabilities. We evaluate 13 modern VLMs
                                                                                     and find that current VLM’s navigation performance drops
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable                                  sharply as mobility constraints tighten, and that even state-
progress in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN), offering                               of-the-art models struggle with obstacle types that require
new possibilities for navigation decision-making that could                          reasoning on spatial dimensions. We conclude by dis-
benefit both robotic platforms and human users. How-                                 cussing the implications for capability-aware navigation
ever, real-world navigation is inherently conditioned by                             and the opportunities for advancing embodied spatial rea-
the agent’s mobility constraints. For example, a sweeping                            soning in future VLMs. The benchmark is available at
robot cannot traverse stairs, while a quadruped can. We                              https://makeabilitylab.github.io/CapNav/

                                                                        Past navigation research has modeled a wide range of mo-
2.1. Vision Language Navigation and Benchmarks                          bility constraints, including accessibility for wheelchair

Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) studies how an agent                   low vision [13, 36, 55], and robotics embodiments such as
follows natural-language instructions using grounded vi-                quadrupeds [19, 27, 32], humanoids [10], and vehicles oper-
sual observations to traverse an environment and reach a                ating over varied terrain [23, 29]. Some works also consider
goal [2, 67]. Since the introduction of Room-to-Room                    settings where multiple mobility profiles co-exist, either
(R2R) [2], which casts indoor navigation as step-by-step ac-            through simulator diversity [58–60] or by modeling user
tion selection on a sparse connectivity graph, a wide range             preferences [28]. Collectively, these studies highlight that
of datasets and benchmarks have expanded VLN along mul-                 embodiment constraints materially change feasible routes
tiple axes. Indoor instruction-following has been scaled in             and navigation strategies.
path length, diversity, and grounding density (e.g., R4R [22]               However, most evaluations remain siloed—focusing on
and RxR [26]); broader urban/street settings have also                  a single embodiment, environment family, or constraint
been explored (e.g., TOUCHDOWN [9], StreetLearn [35],                   type—making cross-embodiment comparison difficult on
CityLearn [7], CityWalker [33], Talk2Nav [53]). Other                   matched tasks. Recent efforts begin to address this gap:
benchmarks couple navigation with object grounding or                   VLN-PE (introduced with a holistic study of physical and
task execution (e.g., REVERIE [39], ALFRED [48], Ob-                    visual disparities) enables systematic cross-embodiment
jectNav [3], EmbodiedBench [64]), while newer efforts                   evaluation in a physically grounded simulator setting [54];
probe long-horizon and open-ended embodied behaviors                    NaviTrace [56] evaluates embodiment-conditioned naviga-
(e.g., GOAT-bench [24] and NavBench [40]).                              tion via 2D trace prediction in real-world images; and

Figure 3. Overview of CapNav’s data construction: Starting from a 3D indoor scan, we manually record a touring video and a navigation
graph. We then use Gemini to generate natural language navigation tasks. Finally, per-task and per-agent traversability are annotated by
manually controlling agents in the annotation interface.

4.3. Failure-mode taxonomy
To characterize systematic errors, we use Gemini-3 to mine
recurring error themes from 1,000 randomly sampled infer-
ence outputs, and then manually refine these themes into a
four-category taxonomy. We then visualize the VLM pre-
dicted results of 1500 sampled QA pairs to measure the
prevalence and distribution of each error type.
Path hallucination: (N = 659 / 1500) the predicted path
links non-adjacent nodes, or violates the specified start/end,
indicating an incorrect reasoning of the scene connectivity.
Obstacle hallucination: (N = 418) the model reports non-
existent blocking obstacles (e.g., closed doors or clutter),
suggesting an unreliable interpretation of visual evidence.
Dimension neglect: (N = 191) the model overlooks ge-
ometric constraints that block the agent (e.g., narrow
doors, tight clearances, cluttered passages), reflecting weak
grounding between spatial extent and traversability.
Ability hallucination: (N = 10) the output reasoning con-
tradicts the provided agent profile. This failure is observed
in smaller open-sourced models (e.g., MiMo-VL 7B).
